inline.s: [Elephants, horses, and the birds and beasts — why are they captured? How do simile and cause perfect the siddhanta, together with the doer and the deed? The thickets, the bewilderment, and the six superknowledges — the mind's measure that does not appear, the grounds that never reach one another, the hundred changes, the hundred non-receptions; the art of medicine, works of craft, and the sciences of the bright knowledge-places.]

Why are elephants, horses, and the various birds and beasts captured? How is it that, relying on simile, the siddhanta is brought to accord? And what of the doer and the deed? The thicket, the bewilderment, the six superknowledges, the mind's measure that does not appear, the grounds that do not reach one another, the hundred changes, the hundred non-receptions; the art of medicine, treatises on craft, and the sciences of the bright knowledge-places — all of these, in the end, are devoid of self-nature.
The Tang translation says:

“Of what cause are elephants and horses? How are they taken? How, relying on simile, is the siddhanta brought to accord? The deed and the doer, the many groves and bewilderment. Such is the principle of reality: mind only, without realms, the grounds without sequence, the signless turning-grounds. The art of medicine, works of craft, and the sciences of the bright knowledge-places.”
Above,
the World-Honored One repeated the various names and marks that Mahamati had asked about,
and pointed out that these
are all illusions devoid of self-nature (“
arriving at self-naturelessness
”). Below, in order to further rouse the
Great

assembly so that they would not squander time and energy entangling themselves in these endless vine-tangles, he answered Mahamati's question in turn with even deeper and finer questions, saying: Why do you not ask about such things?

[Vine-tangles] Vines wrap around a tree until it withers. In the lineages (the Chan school), 'vine-tangles' refers to delighting in verbal language and intellectual analysis, leading people to busy themselves with the karmic consciousness; just as vines spread and interweave, so those who hear are instead bound. Those harmed either waste their time at best or go astray at worst.

[Mountains, the earth, Mount Sumeru, the vast seas, the measure of sun and moon — the beings low, middling, and high: how many particles of dust are in each body? And in each land, how many particles?]

Taking a particle of dust as the unit of volume, measure the mountains, Mount Sumeru, the great seas, the sun and moon, and the beings below, middling, and above: how many particles make up each? And how many particles are there in each land (the great chiliocosm)?

[Particles of dust] The subtlest thing visible to the naked eye. [Beings below, middling, and above] The lower beings are those of the three evil paths — hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts; the middling beings are those of the three wholesome paths — devas, humans, and asuras; the higher beings are those of the three noble paths — sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.
[How many in a bow? How many in an elbow, a pace, a krosa, a half-yojana, a yojana?]
Taking the diameter of a particle of dust as the unit of length, measure each bow, elbow, krosa, and yojana: how many particles make up each?
An old commentary says: two feet make one cubit, four cubits make one bow, five hundred bows make one krosa, and ten krosas make one yojana. The yojana is the same as the yojana (a distance measure).
[Yojana] The unit of distance in India. It has three sizes — great, middling, and small: the great yojana is about eighty li, the middling about sixty li, and the small about forty li.
[How many [dust-particles] in a hare's hair, in a window-dust, in a nit, in a sheep's hair, in a grain of barley?]
Taking a particle of dust as the unit of volume, measure each hare's-hair tip, window-dust, nit, sheep's-hair tip, and grain of barley: how many particles make up each?
[Ji (
jǐ
)] is the egg of the louse [shi (
shī
)]. [Barley (
kuàng
)] is the barley grain.

An old commentary says: seven particles of dust make one window-dust; seven window-dusts make one hare's-hair-tip dust; seven hare's-hair-tip dusts make one sheep's-hair-tip dust; seven sheep's-hair-tip dusts make one ox's-hair-tip dust; seven ox's-hair-tip dusts make one nit; seven nits make one louse; seven lice make one mustard seed; and seven mustard seeds make one grain of barley.
[How many barley grains in a prastha? How many barley grains in an adhaka? In a drona, a nadika, a laksa, and a koti — and down to a vimbaka — how many are in each?]

How many grains of barley are in one prastha (half a dou)? How many in one adhaka (one dou)? In one drona (one hu), one nadika (ten hu), one laksa (a hundred thousand hu), one koti (a hundred million hu), and down to one vimbaka (one zhao hu) — how many grains of barley are in each?
[Hu (
hú
)] ten dou make one hu. [Zhao] In antiquity it meant ten thousand yi, that is, a trillion.

[How many anu make one sarshapa (mustard seed)? How many sarshapa make one laja? How many laja make one masha (bean)? How many masha make one dana? How many dana make one karshapana? How many karshapana make one pala (pound)? These successive aggregates — how many pala make one Sumeru?]

Taking a particle's weight as the unit of weight: how many anu (particles) make one sarshapa (mustard seed)? How many sarshapa make one laja (grass seed)? How many laja make one masha (bean)? How many masha make one dana (zhu)? How many dana make one karshapana (liang)? How many karshapana make one pala (jin)? These successive aggregates — how many pala make one Mount Sumeru? (The Tang translation says:
“How many jin make one Sumeru?”
[Anu (
nóu
)] a particle of dust.
[These are exactly what you should have asked — why need you ask about other things?]
All of these are what you should have asked; why need you ask about other matters?
[The sravakas and pratyekabuddhas, the Buddha and his most victorious sons — how many in each body? Why do you not ask about this!]
The sravakas and pratyekabuddhas, the Buddha and the bodhisattvas — how many are there in all? And how many particles of dust are in each of their bodies? Why do you not ask about these?

[Sravaka] One who attains awakening by hearing the sound of the Buddha's teaching of the Four Noble Truths. [Pratyekabuddha] Also called the independently awakened one: one who, in the Buddha's time, hears the Buddha teach the principle of the twelve links of dependent origination and thereby awakens, and is called a 'pratyekabuddha'; one who, born in a world without a Buddha, contemplates the arising and ceasing of all dharmas through dependent origination and awakens on his own is called a 'solitary awakened one.'
[How many anu in a flame? How many anu again in the wind? How many anu in each of the senses? How many in the pores and the eyebrows?]
How many dust-particles in a blossom of flame
How many in a gust of wind
How many in each hair of the body
And the pores and eyebrows, how many dust-particles
These too are questions
why do you not ask?
Above,
from
Mountains, the earth, Mount Sumeru
” to “how many in the pores and the eyebrows”
, there are thirty-eight lines in all,
asking about
thirty-two
items
of matters,
all of which
Mahamati
had not asked about,
and therefore
the World-Honored One
raises them to ask,
reproaching him: Why do you not ask about these questions?

In fact, the World-Honored One used these questions — utterly unrelated to the self-awakened noble wisdom — to show from the opposite side that everything Mahamati had asked above was idle talk. Master Yongjia's Song of Realizing the Way says:
“All number-sayings and not-number-sayings — what have they to do with my spirit's awareness?”
The realm of the self-awakened noble wisdom realized by the Buddhas is indeed not to be reached by deluded discrimination.

[Idle talk] Speech without practical substance. [All number-sayings and not-number-sayings — what have they to do with my spirit's awareness?] All discrimination of names and marks — what has it to do with the awareness of my own nature? 'Number-sayings, not-number-sayings' here is a metaphor for the discrimination of names and marks. [Discrimination] Attempting to derive reality out of concepts.

blocks.text: The World-Honored One Continues to Answer

inline.s: Below, the World-Honored One again continues to repeat
the remaining part of what Mahamati had asked,
showing even more clearly that, with respect to entering the self-awakened noble wisdom, they are all idle talk.

[Guardian of wealth, the sovereign king, the wheel-turning universal monarch — how does the king protect? What is liberation? The expanded teaching and the pithy saying, as you have asked. The manifold desires of beings, and their manifold foods and drinks. How the grove of men and women, the adamantine mountain? How the illusion-like dream, the wild-deer's simile of craving? How the mountain devas and rishis, adorned by the gandharvas? To where does liberation go? Who is bound, who liberated? How the dhyana realms, the transformations and the non-Buddhist sects? How what is made without a cause, how what is made with a cause? Made with a cause and made without a cause, and the neither-having-nor-not-having cause? How what has now ceased? How to purify the consciousnesses? How the consciousnesses turn, and how they turn the various deeds? How to cut off the notions? How samadhi arises? Who destroys the three realms of existence? In what place, for what body? How, when there is no being, does one speak of 'I' and 'self'? How the worldly speech? I pray you, expound in detail. What is the mark of what is asked, and the non-self of what is asked? How the embryo, and the various other bodies? How to cut off the views of permanence and annihilation? How does the mind attain stillness — speech and the various wisdoms, the precepts, the lineage, the Buddha's sons? How the attainment and the treatise? How the teacher and the disciple? The various beings — how are these? How the food and drink? The wise one, Mara's arrangements? How the trees and the vine-tangles? Asked by the most victorious son. How the various lands? The immortals' long ascetic practice? How the clan names? From what teacher do they receive instruction? How the ugly? How do people cultivate? In the realm of desire, what is not comprehended — the Akanistha accomplished? How the mundane psychic powers? What is a bhikshu? How the nirmana-buddha (the transformation Buddha)? How the sambhoga-buddha (the reward Buddha)? How the tathata-buddha? The Buddha of equality and wisdom? How the assembly (the sangha)? Thus asks the Buddha's son. The harp and the waist-drum, the flower, the lands beyond light. The mind-ground has seven.]

[Akanistha] That is, the Akanistha heaven, translated into Chinese as the Heaven of Ultimate Form. It is one of the eighteen heavens of the realm of form, the very summit of the realm of form, and so is called the Heaven of Ultimate Form. [The mind-ground has seven] The Tang translation says: 'How to cause his mind to dwell in the seven grounds?'

What do these questions above have to do with entering the self-awakened noble wisdom? Answering them is of no benefit. Therefore the World-Honored One merely repeats these questions so that everyone may understand that they are but idle talk.
[All that you have asked is as it truly is — these and the many others that the Buddha's son should ask!]

What you have asked is all that worldly people ponder over. If that is so, then apart from the questions you asked above, there are still a great many others that you too should ask! (This is ironic: if one is still sunk in thought and reckoning, the questions that could be asked are still countless! To count the sands of the sea — how could one hope to gain the treasure?)

blocks.text: The Meaning of the One Hundred Eight Phrases

inline.s: Below, the World-Honored One formally answers the 'one hundred eight meanings' that the bodhisattva Mahamati asked.

[Each mark in mutual accord, far from all the faults of views, the siddhanta beyond words. Now I shall display, establishing the phrases in due order; the Buddha's sons, listen well! These one hundred eight phrases above, as the Buddhas have spoken.]

As to the vast array of all phenomena, one should bring each mark into accord with its real nature (returning the marks to the essence), and so be far from the faults of the views of the two extremes (clearly indicating that what was asked above is the fault of views), because the all-bestowing dharma (the siddhanta of the first meaning) is beyond words. Now I, at the place of wordlessness, will display through words, establishing phrases in due order. O Buddha's sons, listen well and carefully! These one hundred eight phrases below are, as the Buddhas have spoken.
